Introduction

This document accompanies the manuscript “Chimpanzee drumming shows rhythmicity and subspecies variation” Vesta Eleuteri et al. (2025).

Defining bins and coding ratios categories

bins <- list(
  "1" = c(0, 1 / 4.25), # 1 / 4.5
  "2" = c(1 / 4.25, 1 / 3.75), # 1 / 4 > 1:3
  "3" = c(1 / 3.75, 1 / 3.25), # 1 / 3.5
  "4" = c(1 / 3.25, 1 / 2.75), # 1 / 3 > 1:2
  "5" = c(1 / 2.75, 1 / 2.25), # 1 / 2.5
  "6" = c(1 / 2.25, 1 - 1 / 2.25), # 1 / 2 > 1:1
  "7" = c(1 - 1 / 2.25, 1 - 1 / 2.75), # 1 - 1 / 2.5
  "8" = c(1 - 1 / 2.75, 1 - 1 / 3.25), # 1 - 1 / 3 > 2:1
  "9" = c(1 - 1 / 3.25, 1 - 1 / 3.75), # 1 - 1 / 3.5
  "10" = c(1 - 1 / 3.75, 1 - 1 / 4.25), # 1 - 1 / 4 > 3:1
  "11" = c(1 - 1 / 4.25, 1) # 1 - 1 / 4.5
)

breaks <- c(0, 1 / 4.25, 1 / 3.75, 1 / 3.25, 1 / 2.75, 1 / 2.25, 1 - 1 / 2.25, 1 - 1 / 2.75, 1 - 1 / 3.25, 1 - 1 / 3.75, 1 - 1 / 4.25, 1)

labels <- names(bins)

ratios$Bin <- cut(ratios$Ratio, breaks = breaks, labels = labels)
ratios.simulated$Bin <- cut(ratios.simulated$Ratio, breaks = breaks, labels = labels)

Main text: Analyses for non-random timing, isochrony, and shorter-longer adjacent inter-hit intervals in drumming

Introduction

Our main analysis relies on the method devised by Roeske et al. (2020), in which the relationships between adjacent inter-onset/inter-hit intervals (IOIs/IHIs) are described by the formula: \(r_k = \frac{IOI_k}{IOI_k + IOI_{k+1}}\). This formula results in ratios \(r_k\) that range from 0 to 1, where e.g. 0.5 indicates isochrony.

Recently, Jadoul et al. (2025) have highlighted a number of issues with the usual method of doing statistics with these ratios, and have improved the method as hitherto used. Our analysis takes into account these new insights.

Classically, the null hypothesis is that observed IOIs are distributed according to a random uniform distribution. However, the statistical tests that are generally used do not conform to this null hypothesis (Jadoul et al., 2025). According to Jadoul et al. (2025), the assumption of a uniformly random distribution of IOIs as the null-hypothesis means that the ratios are distributed according to the distribution plotted below. The exact shape of this distribution is dependent on the left and right bounds of the random uniform distribution used for sampling the IOIs. However, the shape will remain similar to the one plotted below.

As left (a) and right (b) bounds of the uniform distribution of IOIs, in our analysis we use the minimum observed IOI duration and the maximum observed IOI duration, respectively.

The dotted lines in the plot are the histogram bins, following Roeske et al. (2020), which represent the integer ratios 1:3 (bin centered around 0.25), 1:2 (bin centered around 0.33), 1:1 (isochrony; bin centered around 0.5), 2:1 (bin centered around 0.66), and 3:1 (bin centered around 0.75). The bins in between these integer ratios are the off-integer bins.

ggplot(ratios.simulated, aes(x = Ratio)) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 2) +
  theme_drumming() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = breaks, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5, colour = "grey") +
  labs(x = "Ratio", y = "Probability density", title = "Random ratios distribution", subtitle = "Assumes uniformly random IOIs") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 0.25, 0.3333, 0.5, 0.6666, 0.75, 1), limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("0.0", "0.25\n1:3", "0.33\n1:2", "0.5\n1:1", "0.66\n3:2", "0.75\n3:1", "1.0")
  )

We define the bins following Roeske et al. (2020):

ratios.bins <- data.frame(bin = as.character(1:11))

ratios.bins$bin_left <- sapply(bins, function(x) x[1])
ratios.bins$bin_right <- sapply(bins, function(x) x[2])
ratios.bins$bin_name <- c("", "1/4", "1/3.5", "1/3", "1/2.5", "1/2", "1 - 1/2.5", "1 - 1/3", "1 - 1/3.5", "1 - 1/4", "")
ratios.bins$bin_alternative_name <- c("", "1:3", "", "1:2", "", "1:1", "", "2:1", "", "3:1", "")

kable(ratios.bins,
  format = "html", caption = "Bins definition", col.names =
    c("Bin", "Bin (left bound)", "Bin (right bound)", "Bin center", "Integer ratio")
) %>%
  kable_styling("striped", full_width = FALSE)

Then, we count the number of observations in each bin.

# Code off- and on-isochronous
ratios$On_off_isoc <- NA
ratios$On_off_isoc <- factor(ratios$On_off_isoc, levels = c("Off", "On", "Other"))
ratios$On_off_isoc <- "Other"
ratios$On_off_isoc[ratios$Bin %in% c(5, 7)] <- "Off"
ratios$On_off_isoc[ratios$Bin == 6] <- "On"

# Count
ratios.isoc.counts <- dplyr::summarize(dplyr::group_by(ratios, Subspecies, Population, Community, Com_indiv_code),
  On_isochronous = sum(On_off_isoc == "On"), Off_isochronous = sum(On_off_isoc == "Off"), Other = sum(On_off_isoc == "Other"), Total_obs = n()
)

Statistics

Here we test:

  1. Whether the drumming ratios are randomly distributed (i.e. whether the distribution of observed ratios is different from a distribution of ratios derived from uniformly random inter-hit intervals).
  2. Whether the distributions of eastern and western differ from each other.
  3. Whether there are more on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance.
  4. Whether there are more on-isochronous ratios in eastern vs. western chimpanzees.
  5. Whether there is more alternation of shorter-longer inter-hit intervals in eastern vs. western chimpanzees.

Do chimpanzees show non-random timing in drumming?

Here we answer the question: “Is the drumming random?” by comparing the distributions of observed ratios with the distribution of ratios as expected when inter-hit intervals (IHIs) are uniformly randomly distributed (which we simulated above). We use Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for this purpose.

All observations (both eastern and western chimpanzee drumming) vs. uniformly random

ks.all <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio, ratios.simulated$Ratio, alternative = "two.sided")
ks.all

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio and ratios.simulated$Ratio
D = 0.06502, p-value = 4.451e-07
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

Across subspecies, for all chimpanzees the drumming is not random.

Western chimpanzee vs. uniformly random

ks.wac <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"], ratios.simulated$Ratio, alternative = "two.sided")
ks.wac

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"] and ratios.simulated$Ratio
D = 0.088789, p-value = 4.26e-09
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

For western chimpanzees the drumming is not random.

Eastern chimpanzees vs. uniformly random

ks.eac <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"], ratios.simulated$Ratio, alternative = "two.sided")
ks.eac

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"] and ratios.simulated$Ratio
D = 0.091761, p-value = 0.0002008
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

For eastern chimpanzees the drumming is not random.

Do eastern and western chimpanzees show different distributions of ratios?

ks.eac.vs.wac <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"], ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"], alternative = "two.sided")
ks.eac.vs.wac

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"] and ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"]
D = 0.14976, p-value = 7.184e-08
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

Eastern and western chimpanzees show different distributions of ratios.

Do chimpanzees show isochrony in drumming?

Here we compare the proportion of on-isochronous ratios that were observed to the number of on-isochronous ratios that can be expected by chance (i.e., when assuming uniformly random IHIs).

We convert the number of on-isochronous observations to probabilities using: \(\frac{\textrm{number of isochronous observations}}{\textrm{total number of observations}}\). We do this for each individual chimpanzee separately. The individuals’ probabilities are then compared to chance probability using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Chance probability was calculated using the formula provided by Jadoul et al. (2025):

\[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{(4b - 5a)^2}{40 (b - a)^2}\]

This yielded a value of 0.2042091.

# Calculate the surface area of the isochronous bin using the formula from Jadoul et al. (2025)
a <- min(ibis$IBI_ms)
b <- max(ibis$IBI_ms)
surface_area_isochronous <- ((1 / 2) - (((4 * b - 5 * a)^2) / (40 * (b - a)^2)))

# Multiply by two (there's one bin on each side of 0.5 when using this formula)
surface_area_isochronous <- surface_area_isochronous * 2 # 0.2042091

# Subtract surface area of isochronous bin from empirical probabilities
ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob <- ratios.isoc.counts$On_isochronous / ratios.isoc.counts$Total_obs
ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized <- ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob - surface_area_isochronous
set.seed(2)
ggplot(ratios.isoc.counts, aes(y = Isoc_prob * 100, x = Subspecies, fill = Subspecies)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_drumming() +
  labs(
    y = "", x = "",
  title = "") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = surface_area_isochronous * 100, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(scale = 1))

ggsave(here("plots", "isochronous_ratios_vs_random.pdf"), width = 7, height = 5)
ggsave(here("plots", "isochronous_ratios_vs_random.png"), width = 7, height = 5)
ggsave(here("plots", "isochronous_ratios_vs_random.svg"), width = 7, height = 5)

All observations (both eastern and western chimpanzee drumming)

isoc.vs.random.wsrt.all <- wilcox.test(ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized, alternative = "two.sided")
isoc.vs.random.wsrt.all

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized
V = 606, p-value = 0.6604
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0
print(paste("Median for all chimps:", median(ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized)))
[1] "Median for all chimps: 0.0180131260429715"

Across subspecies, there are not more on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance.

Western chimpanzees

isoc.vs.random.wsrt.wac <- wilcox.test(ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"],
  alternative = "two.sided"
) # Significant
isoc.vs.random.wsrt.wac

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

V = 281, p-value = 0.007656
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0

[1] "Median for Western: 0.0531222821198695"

In Western chimpanzees, there are significantly more on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance.

Eastern chimpanzees

isoc.vs.random.wsrt.eac <- wilcox.test(ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"],
  alternative = "two.sided"

isoc.vs.random.wsrt.eac

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
V = 58, p-value = 0.04697
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0
print(paste("Median for Eastern:", median(ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"])))

In Eastern chimpanzees, there are significantly fewer on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance.

Is there more isochrony in eastern vs. western chimpanzees?

Here we compare the empirical probabilities (i.e. \(\frac{\textrm{number of isochronous observations}}{\textrm{total number of observations}}\)) of on-isochronous ratios between eastern and western chimpanzees using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

wilcox.test(
  ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"],
  ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
)

    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"] and ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
W = 403, p-value = 0.005526
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
print(paste("Median for East:", median(ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"])))
[1] "Median for East: 0.111111111111111"
print(paste("Median for West:", median(ratios.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"])))
[1] "Median for West: 0.25733137829912"

There are more on-isochronous ratios in western than in eastern chimpanzees.

Do eastern chimpanzees alternate shorter-longer inter-hit intervals more than western chimpanzees?

We first extract the lag-one autocorrelations values by subspecies and drumming bout

acf.cv <- ddply(ibis, .(Subspecies, Population, Community, Individual, Drumming_bout, N_hits), summarize,
    lag_one = acf(IBI, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],
    cv = sd(IBI) / mean(IBI)
)

acf.cv.bysubspecies <- ddply(acf.cv, .(Subspecies), summarize,
    mean_lag_one = mean(lag_one, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_lag_one = sd(lag_one, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_cv = mean(cv, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_cv = sd(cv, na.rm = TRUE)
)

kable(acf.cv.bysubspecies, format = "html", escape = FALSE) %>%
    kable_styling("striped", full_width = FALSE)
Subspecies mean_lag_one sd_lag_one mean_cv sd_cv
Western -0.2191087 0.2726113 0.5354646 0.3366030
Eastern -0.3867767 0.2837444 0.7766807 0.3768942

We then plot the lag-one autocorrelations

ggplot(acf.cv, aes(y = Subspecies, x = lag_one, colour = Subspecies)) +
    stat_summary(geom = "pointrange", show.legend = FALSE) +
    theme_drumming() +
    labs(y = "", x = "") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.5, 0)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.5, -0.25, 0)) +
    theme(
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Make panel background transparent
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Make plot background transparent
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(), # Remove major grid lines
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), # Remove minor grid lines
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray80", size = 0.5), # Add vertical major grid lines
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), # Remove major horizontal grid lines
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Make legend background transparent
        legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA) # Make legend box background transparent
    )

Then we compare the lag-one autocorrelations by subspecies using a t-test

# Check equality of variances
acf.east <- acf.cv$lag_one[acf.cv$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
acf.west <- acf.cv$lag_one[acf.cv$Subspecies == "Western"]
var.test(acf.east, acf.west)

    F test to compare two variances

data:  acf.east and acf.west
F = 1.0833, num df = 160, denom df = 208, p-value = 0.5858
alternative hypothesis: true ratio of variances is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.8109689 1.4553998
sample estimates:
ratio of variances 
          1.083345 
# Run t-test
acf.t.test <- t.test(acf.east, acf.west)

# ACF by subspecies
acf.by.subspecies <- as.data.frame(list(
    test_statistic = acf.t.test$statistic,
    p_value = acf.t.test$p.value,
    cohens_d = mean(acf.east, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(acf.west, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt((var(acf.east, na.rm = TRUE) + var(acf.west, na.rm = TRUE)) / 2),
    df = acf.t.test$parameter,
    method = acf.t.test$method
))

kable(acf.by.subspecies, format = "html", escape = FALSE) %>%
    kable_styling("striped", full_width = FALSE)
test_statistic p_value cohens_d df method
t -5.731945 0 0.4007224 337.2659 Welch Two Sample t-test

Eastern chimpanzees alternate shorter and longer inter-hit intervals in drumming more often than western chimpanzees.

Main text: Analysis for subspecies variation in drumming tempo

Do western chimpanzees drum with a faster tempo than eastern chimpanzees?

We first extract the drumming tempo per drumming bout and make a drumming tempo plot

tempi <- ddply(ibis, .(Subspecies, Population, Community, Individual, Drumming_bout), summarize,
  tempo = mean(IBI_ms)
)

ggplot(tempi, aes(x = Subspecies, y = tempo, fill = Subspecies)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE, alpha = 0.7, position = position_jitter(width=0.1)) +
  labs(y = "Tempo [ms]", title = "Subspecies drumming tempo") +
  theme_drumming() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 40),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 34),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 34),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 30),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 34, hjust=1),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 34, hjust=1),
    legend.position = "none",  
    legend.key.size = unit(1, "cm"),

Preparations

We subset the data to only include drumming bouts with 5 or more hits.

ratios.5plushits <- ratios
ratios.5plushits <- ratios.5plushits %>%
  group_by(Drumming_bout) %>%
  filter(n() >= 3) %>% # remove drums < 3 ratios.5plushits (4 IBIs/5 beats)
  group_by(Com_indiv_code) %>% # remove individuals with <3 drums
  filter(n_distinct(Drumming_bout) >= 3) %>%
  group_by(Community) %>% # remove communities with <1 individual
  filter(n_distinct(Individual) > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

Below, we count the number of empirical observations in each bin for drumming bouts with 5 hits or more.

# Code off- and on-isochronous
ratios.5plushits$On_off_isoc <- NA
ratios.5plushits$On_off_isoc <- factor(ratios.5plushits$On_off_isoc, levels = c("Off", "On", "Other"))
ratios.5plushits$On_off_isoc <- "Other"
ratios.5plushits$On_off_isoc[ratios.5plushits$Bin %in% c(5, 7)] <- "Off"
ratios.5plushits$On_off_isoc[ratios.5plushits$Bin == 6] <- "On"

# Count
ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts <- dplyr::summarize(dplyr::group_by(ratios.5plushits, Subspecies, Population, Community, Com_indiv_code),
  On_isochronous = sum(On_off_isoc == "On"), Off_isochronous = sum(On_off_isoc == "Off"), Other = sum(On_off_isoc == "Other"), Total_obs = n()
)

Statistics

Do chimpanzees show non-random timing in drumming bouts with >=5 hits? (drumming ratios vs. random distribution)

Here we answer the question: “Is the drumming random?” by comparing the distributions of observed ratios with the distribution of ratios as expected when inter-hit intervals (IHIs) are uniformly randomly distributed. We use the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for this purpose.

All observations (both eastern and western chimpanzee drumming) vs. uniformly random

ks.all <- ks.test(ratios.5plushits$Ratio, ratios.simulated$Ratio, alternative = "two.sided")
ks.all

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios.5plushits$Ratio and ratios.simulated$Ratio
D = 0.071078, p-value = 2.128e-06
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

Across subspecies, for all chimpanzees the drumming bouts with 5 or more hits are not random.

Eastern chimpanzees vs. uniformly random

ks.eac <- ks.test(ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Eastern"], ratios.simulated$Ratio, alternative = "two.sided")
ks.eac

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Eastern"] and ratios.simulated$Ratio
D = 0.043395, p-value = 0.5215
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

For eastern chimpanzees, the drumming bouts with 5 or more hits are random.

Western chimpanzees vs. uniformly random

ks.wac <- ks.test(ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Western"], ratios.simulated$Ratio, alternative = "two.sided")
ks.wac

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Western"] and ratios.simulated$Ratio
D = 0.08542, p-value = 7.944e-07
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

For western chimpanzees, the drumming bouts with 5 or more hits are not random.

Do eastern and western chimpanzees show different distributions of ratios?

ks.eac.vs.wac <- ks.test(ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Eastern"],
  ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Western"],
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
ks.eac.vs.wac

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Eastern"] and ratios.5plushits$Ratio[ratios.5plushits$Subspecies == "Western"]
D = 0.085806, p-value = 0.04278
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

Eastern and western chimpanzees show different distributions of ratios in drumming bouts with 5 or more hits.

Are there more on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance?

Here we compare the proportion of on-isochronous ratios that were observed to the number of on-isochronous ratios that can be expected by chance (i.e., when assuming uniformly random IHIs).

We convert the number of on-isochronous observations to probabilities using: \(\frac{\textrm{number of isochronous observations}}{\textrm{total number of observations}}\). We do this for each individual chimpanzee separately. The individuals’ probabilities are then compared to chance probability using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Chance probability was calculated using the formula provided by Jadoul et al. (2025):

\[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{(4b - 5a)^2}{40 (b - a)^2}\]

# Calculate the surface area of the isochronous bin using the formula from Jadoul et al. (2025)
a <- min(ibis$IBI_ms)
b <- max(ibis$IBI_ms)
surface_area_isochronous <- ((1 / 2) - (((4 * b - 5 * a)^2) / (40 * (b - a)^2)))

# Multiply by two (there's one bin on each side of 0.5 when using this formula)
surface_area_isochronous <- surface_area_isochronous * 2 # 0.2042091

# Subtract surface area of isochronous bin from empirical probabilities
ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob <- ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$On_isochronous / ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Total_obs
ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized <- ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob - surface_area_isochronous
ggplot(ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts, aes(y = Isoc_prob * 100, x = Subspecies, fill = Subspecies)) +
  geom_boxplot(colour = "black", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_drumming() +
  labs(
    y = "Percentage of isochronous drumming ratios per individual", x = "Subspecies",
    title = "Percentage of isochronous ratios compared to chance level",
    subtitle = "Chance level indicated by dotted line is based on uniformly randomly distributed IOIs.\nOnly drumming bouts with 5 or more hits are included.",
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = surface_area_isochronous * 100, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(scale = 1))

All observations (both eastern and western chimpanzee drumming)

isoc.vs.random.wsrt.all <- wilcox.test(ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized, alternative = "two.sided")
isoc.vs.random.wsrt.all

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized
V = 248, p-value = 0.5165
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0
print(paste("Median for all chimps:", median(ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized)))
[1] "Median for all chimps: 0.0211430164968056"

Across subspecies, for all chimpanzees there are not more on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance in drumming bouts with 5 or more hits.

Eastern chimpanzees

isoc.vs.random.wsrt.eac <- wilcox.test(ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"], alternative = "two.sided") # Significant
isoc.vs.random.wsrt.eac

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
V = 23, p-value = 0.2238
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0
print(paste("Median for Eastern:", median(ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"])))
[1] "Median for Eastern: -0.0873259792961339"

In eastern chimpanzees, there are not more or fewer on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance in drumming bouts with 5 or more hits.

Western chimpanzees

isoc.vs.random.wsrt.wac <- wilcox.test(ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"], alternative = "two.sided") # Significant
isoc.vs.random.wsrt.wac

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"]
V = 127, p-value = 0.01792
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 0
print(paste("Median for Western:", median(ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob_normalized[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"])))
[1] "Median for Western: 0.0544115934759217"

In western chimpanzees, there are significantly more on-isochronous ratios than expected by chance in drumming bouts with 5 or more hits.

Is there more isochrony in eastern vs. western chimpanzees?

Here we compare the empirical probabilities (i.e. \(\frac{\textrm{number of isochronous observations}}{\textrm{total number of observations}}\)) of on-isochronous ratios between eastern and western chimpanzees using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test.

wilcox.test(
  ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"],
  ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
)

    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Western"] and ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Isoc_prob[ratios.5plushits.isoc.counts$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
W = 149, p-value = 0.03944
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

There are more on-isochronous ratios in western than in eastern chimpanzees in drumming bouts with 5 or more hits.

Do eastern chimpanzees alternate shorter-longer inter-hit intervals more than western chimpanzees?

We subset the data to only include drumming bouts with 5 or more hits.

ibis.5plushits <- ibis
ibis.5plushits <- ibis.5plushits %>%
  group_by(Drumming_bout) %>%
  filter(n() >= 4) %>% # remove drums < 4 IHIs
  group_by(Com_indiv_code) %>% # remove individuals with <3 drums
  filter(n_distinct(Drumming_bout) >= 3) %>%
  group_by(Community) %>% # remove communities with <1 individual
  filter(n_distinct(Individual) > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

We first extract the lag-one autocorrelations values by subspecies and drumming bout

acf.cv.5plushits <- ddply(ibis.5plushits, .(Subspecies, Population, Community, Individual, Drumming_bout, N_hits), summarize,
    lag_one = acf(IBI, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],
    cv = sd(IBI) / mean(IBI)
)

acf.cv.bysubspecies.5plushits <- ddply(acf.cv.5plushits, .(Subspecies), summarize,
    mean_lag_one = mean(lag_one, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_lag_one = sd(lag_one, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_cv = mean(cv, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_cv = sd(cv, na.rm = TRUE)
)

kable(acf.cv.bysubspecies.5plushits, format = "html", escape = FALSE) %>%
    kable_styling("striped", full_width = FALSE)
Subspecies mean_lag_one sd_lag_one mean_cv sd_cv
Western -0.1586376 0.2740611 0.5876118 0.3379219
Eastern -0.2438245 0.3234483 0.7515695 0.3721057

We then plot the lag-one autocorrelations

ggplot(acf.cv.5plushits, aes(y = Subspecies, x = lag_one, colour = Subspecies)) +
    stat_summary(geom = "pointrange", show.legend = FALSE) +
    theme_drumming() +
    labs(y = "", x = "") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.5, 0)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.5, -0.25, 0)) +
    theme(
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Make panel background transparent
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Make plot background transparent
        panel.grid.major = element_blank(), # Remove major grid lines
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), # Remove minor grid lines
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "gray80", size = 0.5), # Add vertical major grid lines
        panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), # Remove major horizontal grid lines
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA), # Make legend background transparent
        legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", color = NA) # Make legend box background transparent
    )

Then we compare the lag-one autocorrelations by subspecies using a t-test

# Check equality of variances
acf.5plushits.east <- acf.cv.5plushits$lag_one[acf.cv.5plushits$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
acf.5plushits.west <- acf.cv.5plushits$lag_one[acf.cv.5plushits$Subspecies == "Western"]
var.test(acf.5plushits.east, acf.5plushits.west)

    F test to compare two variances

data:  acf.5plushits.east and acf.5plushits.west
F = 1.3929, num df = 63, denom df = 139, p-value = 0.1107
alternative hypothesis: true ratio of variances is not equal to 1
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.9272041 2.1652013
sample estimates:
ratio of variances 
          1.392884 
# Run t-test
acf.5plushits.t.test <- t.test(acf.5plushits.east, acf.5plushits.west)

# ACF by subspecies
acf.5plushits.by.subspecies <- as.data.frame(list(
    test_statistic = acf.5plushits.t.test$statistic,
    p_value = acf.5plushits.t.test$p.value,
    cohens_d = mean(acf.5plushits.east, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(acf.5plushits.west, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt((var(acf.5plushits.east, na.rm = TRUE) +
        var(acf.5plushits.west, na.rm = TRUE)) / 2),
    df = acf.5plushits.t.test$parameter,
    method = acf.5plushits.t.test$method
))

Supplement: Analyses for non-random timing and isochrony fully replicating previous studies

Introduction

We here use the method as has been used until now in the literature, which, due to the normalization procedure (i.e. dividing by the bin width rather than the bin surface area), assumes exponentially distributed IHIs/IOIs resulting from a Poisson point-process (Jadoul et al., 2025).

Defining bins, bin widths, etc.

ratios.normalization <- data.frame(bin = as.character(1:11))
ratios.normalization$surface_area <- NA
for (i in 1:11) {
  bin <- bins[[as.character(i)]]
  ratios.normalization$surface_area[ratios.normalization$bin == as.character(i)] <- length(ratios.simulated$Ratio[ratios.simulated$Ratio >= bin[1] &
    ratios.simulated$Ratio < bin[2]]) / length(ratios.simulated$Ratio)
}
ratios.normalization$bin_left <- sapply(bins, function(x) x[1])
ratios.normalization$bin_right <- sapply(bins, function(x) x[2])
ratios.normalization$bin_size <- ratios.normalization$bin_right - ratios.normalization$bin_left
ratios.normalization$bin_name <- c("1/4.5", "1/4", "1/3.5", "1/3", "1/2.5", "1/2", "1 - 1/2", "1 - 1/3", "1 - 1/3.5", "1 - 1/4", "1 - 1/4.5")
ratios.normalization$bin_alternative_name <- c("", "1:3", "", "1:2", "", "1:1", "", "2:1", "", "3:1", "")

Counting the number of empirical observations in each bin and normalize

Below, we count the number of empirical observations in each bin and normalize them by dividing by the bin width.

# Code off- and on-isochronous
ratios$On_off_isoc <- NA
ratios$On_off_isoc <- factor(ratios$On_off_isoc, levels = c("Off", "On", "Other"))
ratios$On_off_isoc <- "Other"
ratios$On_off_isoc[ratios$Bin %in% c(5, 7)] <- "Off"
ratios$On_off_isoc[ratios$Bin == 6] <- "On"

# Count
ratios.isoc.counts.poiss <- dplyr::summarize(dplyr::group_by(ratios, Subspecies, Population, Community, Com_indiv_code),
  On_isochronous = sum(On_off_isoc == "On"), Off_isochronous = sum(On_off_isoc == "Off"), Other = sum(On_off_isoc == "Other"), Total_obs = n()
)

# Normalize
ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm <- ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous / (ratios.normalization$bin_size[6] * ratios.isoc.counts$Total_obs)
ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Off_isochronous_norm <- ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Off_isochronous /
  ((ratios.normalization$bin_size[5] + ratios.normalization$bin_size[7]) * ratios.isoc.counts$Total_obs)
ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Other_norm <- ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Other / ((1 - sum(ratios.normalization$bin_size[5:7])) * ratios.isoc.counts$Total_obs)

The values in the normalized columns represent how much more above chance level the observed counts are. For example, a value of 1.0 means that the observed counts are as expected by chance, a value of 2.0 means that the observed counts are twice what was expected by chance, and so on.

Statistics

Do chimpanzees drum with non-random timing (drumming ratios vs. random distribution)?

Here we answer the question: “Is the drumming random?” by comparing the distributions of observed ratios with the distribution of ratios as expected when IHIs/IOIs are exponentially distributed (i.e. resulting from a Poisson point-process). We use the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for this purpose.

All observations (both eastern and western chimpanzee drumming) vs. Poisson-assumed

ks.all.poiss <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio, "punif")
ks.all.poiss

    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio
D = 0.15463, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

Across subspecies, for all chimpanzees the drumming is not random.

Eastern chimpanzees vs. Poisson-assumed

ks.eac.poiss <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"], "punif")
ks.eac.poiss

    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
D = 0.10079, p-value = 2.982e-05
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

For eastern chimpanzees, the drumming is not random.

Western chimpanzees vs. Poisson-assumed

ks.wac.poiss <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"], "punif")
ks.wac.poiss

    Asymptotic one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"]
D = 0.17843, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

For western chimpanzees, the drumming is not random.

Do eastern and western chimpanzees show different distributions of ratios?

This of course does not depend on the null hypothesis of how the IHIs are distributed but is included here for completeness (as also done in the previous section).

ks.eac.vs.wac.poiss <- ks.test(ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"], ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"])
ks.eac.vs.wac.poiss

    Asymptotic two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

data:  ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Eastern"] and ratios$Ratio[ratios$Subspecies == "Western"]
D = 0.14976, p-value = 7.184e-08
alternative hypothesis: two-sided

Eastern and western chimpanzees show different distributions of ratios.

More on-isochronous vs. off-isochronous?

Here we use the the classic method of comparing the number of on-isochronous vs. off-isochronous ratios, using the (until now common method for) normalization such that we divide by the bin width (which assumes exponentially distributed IHIs/IOIs resulting from a Poissant point-process).

All observations (both eastern and western chimpanzee drumming)

# Paired Wilcoxon test
wilcox.test(ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm, ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Off_isochronous_norm, paired = TRUE)

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm and ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Off_isochronous_norm
V = 751, p-value = 0.002866
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

Using the standard normalization procedure (i.e. dividing by bin width), we find that there are more on-isochronous ratios than off-isochronous ratios across subspecies.

Eastern chimpanzees

wilcox.test(ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Eastern"],
  ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Off_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Eastern"],
  paired = TRUE
)

    Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Eastern"] and ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Off_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
V = 118, p-value = 0.1634
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

Using the standard normalization procedure (i.e. dividing by bin width), we find that there are not more on-isochronous ratios than off-isochronous ratios in eastern chimpanzees.

Western chimpanzees

wilcox.test(ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Western"],
  ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Off_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Western"],

V = 279, p-value = 0.007291
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

Using the standard normalization procedure (i.e. dividing by bin width), we find that there are not more on-isochronous ratios than off-isochronous ratios in western chimpanzees.

Are there more on-isochronous ratios in western than in eastern chimpanzees?

wilcox.test(
  ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Western"],
  ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$On_isochronous_norm[ratios.isoc.counts.poiss$Subspecies == "Eastern"]
)

W = 403, p-value = 0.005526

Using the standard normalization procedure (i.e. dividing by bin width), we find that there are more on-isochronous ratios in western chimpanzees than in eastern chimpanzees.
